# Vaccine and Anti PD1 Study In Dogs with Oral Malignant Melanoma

The University of Florida College of Veterinary Medicine is currently recruiting dogs recently diagnosed with malignant melanoma for a clinical research trial. Dogs must have not had the oral tumor excised to qualify.

  * Inclusion Criteria: Any dog recently diagnosed with oral malignant melanoma that is resectable or minimal and does not have other life threatening diseases. Dogs must have not had the oral tumor excised to qualify.
  * Treatment: Participation involves an initial staging visit and 5 follow up visits. The vaccine will be given 4 times approximately 4 weeks apart followed by 2 restaging visits. Enrolled dogs will receive an intravenous administration via an IV catheter in their leg of the Anti-PD1 antibody (Gilvetmab) at enrollment and then with each subsequent GD2/3 vaccine; for a total of 4 infusions. Booster vaccines will also be available 6 months after completion of the entire vaccine series at an additional charge.   * Contact:  Contact the Oncology Staff at (352) 392-2235 to schedule an evaluation, or complete the Study Interest Form to see if your dog qualifies.

Background:

Melanoma is a devastating cancer in humans and animals (both cats and dogs) with few options for treatment, outside of surgery and radiation. Melanoma often likes to spread to the lungs (metastasis) which can ultimately result in the passing of the person or pet. Through years of research, we have determined that dogs with naturally occurring melanoma, which is not induced by the sun, may be treated with immunotherapy. Immunotherapy is a form of treatment which uses the body’s own immune system to target and fight cancer. We developed a GD3 (ganglioside) based vaccine which has shown in past studies to improve time-to-progression of disease and overall survival in 75% patients in addition to standard of care (surgery or radiation). Our objective in continuing our research with this vaccine is to provide answers (more treatment) for the 25% of canines that don’t respond. To this end we recently added GD2 as an additional component to the vaccine (now a GD2/3 vaccine). We are also now, incorporating the anti-PD1 antibody (Gilvetmab) with the vaccine. The hope is that we can improve outcomes for our patients via this clinical trial designed to treat dogs with naturally occurring melanoma with the administration of the GD2/3 melanoma vaccine and infusions of Gilvetmab. 

Study Interest Form

Oncology Referral Form (**REQUIRED**)

# Canine RNA-Nanoparticle Vaccine Combined with Anti-PD1 Drug Against Osteosarcoma for Canine Patients (Currently Enrolling)

Canine RNA-nanoparticle Vaccine with Anti PD1 drug Against Osteosarcoma for Canine Patients

The University of Florida College of Veterinary Medicine is currently recruiting dogs recently diagnosed with appendicular osteosarcoma for a clinical research trial.  This investigational trial is for the development of a vaccine for the future treatment of appendicular osteosarcoma in dogs.

Enrollment Status: Currently Enrolling 

Inclusion Criteria: Dogs that have been diagnosed with osteosarcoma of a limb based on microscopic confirmation following biopsy. Cells from your dog’s tumor will be collected as a part of a biopsy at the University of Florida Veterinary Hospitals. These cells will be used for the RNA-nanoparticle cancer vaccine creation. Dogs which qualify for the study must receive radiation therapy. The core biopsy (or collection of tumor cells) must occur prior to radiation for vaccine production.

# Phase II Open-label Non-randomized Multicenter Clinical Trial of Trametinib for Dogs With Histiocytic Sarcoma

The University of Florida College of Veterinary Medicine is currently recruiting dogs diagnosed with Histiocytic Sarcoma for a clinical research trial.

Enrollment Criteria: Currently Enrolling

  * Inclusion Criteria: Your dog has been diagnosed with Histiocytic Sarcoma
  * Treatment: Prior to treatment with the study drug (trametinib), a tumor biopsy, and a blood sample (less than one ounce) will be collected. A tumor biopsy will be taken only when tumors are accessible, via a small incision through the skin, and collection of a small piece of tumor tissue, with the patient under sedation. Enrolled dogs will have a physical examination, laboratory analysis, blood pressure measurement, and diagnostic imaging (x-rays and ultrasound). Trametinib will be given by mouth, once daily, as long as your dog is responding to treatment

  * Cost: This study will cover the costs of the Trametinib medication, recheck physical examination fees, collection of blood and tumor samples for investigation, and routine laboratory tests/diagnostic imaging (thoracic radiographs and abdominal ultrasound) at scheduled recheck study visits.
  * Contact: Please complete the Study Interest Form for more information.
  * PI: Dr. Marilia Takada and Dr. Paulo Vilar Saavedra

Background: The purpose of this research is to investigate a new anti-cancer drug, trametinib, that specifically ‘targets’ growth signals found in cancer cells from companion (pet) dogs. This study will determine the anti-tumor efficacy of trametinib in dogs with histiocytic sarcoma. We will measure and document how much the cancer shrinks upon treatment, and how the drug helps improve the patients’ outcome and life expectancy. Additionally, the study will test whether markers in the genes within the tumor can predict the response from treatment, which in the future can help select those dogs that are more likely to respond positively to treatment. Finally, in a simple blood test we will determine whether effective drug levels are present in the patient.

## Osteosarcoma Clinical Trial in Dogs

Current Status: Open and enrolling
Principal Investigators: Dara L. Kraitchman, V.M.D., Ph.D., F.A.C.C., [email protected]

To find out more about this clinical trial, send an email to [email protected] or call 410-502-7325.

  * ### [Button: Summary]

To assess the effectiveness of cryoablation or an investigational immunotherapy to treat osteosarcoma of the appendicular skeleton. Cryoablation is a technique to freeze tumors that may kill the tumor, alleviate pain, and assist the body in rejecting cancer that has spread. Immunotherapy is used as a means to create an in-situ cancer vaccine towards the tumor. Either treatment is performed prior to amputation.

  * ### [Button: Funding and Support]

The cryotherapy or immunotherapy and imaging to look for cancer spread or metastasis is fully funded. Any medications our veterinarians prescribe to alleviate the side effects of the procedure, as well as follow-up imaging and blood tests will also be covered by the study. 
  * ### [Button: Trial Timeline]

Eligible dogs will receive a PET-CT scan and will receive cryotherapy alone or two doses of tumor-injected immunotherapy.  Amputation is required at approximately 2 weeks after treatment followed by chemotherapy.  CT or PET-CT scans will be obtained at 3, 6, and 12 months after treatment Further monitoring will be performed as deemed necessary by CIGAT veterinarians.

# Open veterinary clinical trials are currently recruiting

The Cornell University Hospital for Animals is actively engaged in clinical studies that work towards applicable treatments and cures for our patients. Please consider informing owners of eligible patients about relevant studies, and help us move the research forward!

#### Featured Trial:  Pain treatment for canine cancer patients

  * BACKGROUND: Some dogs with cancer, especially end-stage cancer patients or patients with dermatitis secondary to radiation therapy, experience pain that cannot be adequately controlled with oral medications given by their owners at home. Depending on the site of pain, an epidural injection can provide pain relief superior to oral medications, sometimes with fewer side effects. The duration of pain relief is variable but may last several weeks. Repeating the injection requires heavy sedation or general anesthesia each time, and this puts the dog at risk for anesthetic complications, is time consuming, and can be prohibitively expensive.

# Clinical Trials for Dogs with Cancer

Links last verified: August 20, 2026

## Explore Current Research Trials in Canine Oncology

When a beloved dog is diagnosed with cancer, many families ask whether a clinical trial may provide an additional option. Canine oncology studies are conducted throughout the United States and around the world, but identifying an appropriate trial, and participating in one, can sometimes be challenging.

Each clinical trial has specific eligibility requirements.

These may include: 

  * A dog’s breed
  * Age
  * Weight
  * Overall health
  * Life expectancy
  * Cancer type
  * Cancer stage
  * Previous care
  * ...and other medical factors

Meeting a study’s general description does not guarantee acceptance. Pet parents should speak directly with the research team and their veterinary care provider to determine whether a trial may be appropriate for their dog.

It is also important to understand that clinical trials are not always free.

Research funding may cover only certain tests, medications, procedures, or appointments. Families may still be responsible for additional veterinary expenses, travel, lodging, and repeated visits over several weeks or months, especially when a study is located far from home.

The following links are intended to help pet parents and veterinary professionals find information about current canine oncology trials being conducted throughout the United States and, in some cases, internationally.

We encourage families to carefully review each study’s eligibility requirements, location, potential costs, time commitment, and possible benefits and risks with their veterinary team.

Search the AVMA Veterinary Clinical Trials Registry

## Start Here: Nationwide Search Tools

If you are not sure where to begin, start with the AVMA registry. It lets you search by cancer type and by location, which is faster than checking individual centers one at a time.

#### AVMA Veterinary Clinical Trials Registry

The AVMA Veterinary Clinical Trials Registry, formerly known as the AVMA Animal Health Studies Database, helps dog parents and veterinary professionals find veterinary clinical studies taking place throughout the United States and Canada.

Clinical trials

How can I find an ongoing clinical trial?

Via the search button, you can perform a targeted search for canine clinical trials. In order to do this, tick -if known- the box of your dog’s tumour type (‘Select tumour type’) and/or the countries (‘Select location’) for which you wish to know whether clinical trials are ongoing.

Afterwards, a list of trials for which your dog might be eligible will appear. The listed information is limited to

  * Treatment centre where the trial is available
  * In/exclusion criteria. Inclusion criteria describe the criteria necessary for your dog to participate in the trial (e.g. inoperable tumour). Exclusion criteria describe conditions that exclude possible participation to the trial (e.g. concomitant chemotherapy).
  * Contact information: phone number and e-mail address of the trial’s contact person, webpage with more information on the trial.

For more details on the trial, we recommend you to contact the researchers via the listed contact info.

# Spontaneous tumors in dogs and cats in Algeria: a dual-source descriptive study of practitioner-reported patterns and histopathology-submitted cases

## Abstract

### Background

Algeria has no documented national companion-animal cancer registry, and limited information is available on tumors encountered in veterinary practice or reaching histopathological confirmation. This dual-source descriptive study combined two independently analyzed components: a histopathology-based descriptive case series of diagnostic tumor submissions from dogs and cats, and a cross-sectional questionnaire survey of veterinarians practicing in Algeria. The first component characterized tumors reaching histopathological confirmation, whereas the second examined practitioner-reported tumor patterns, perceived diagnostic-resource availability, and self-reported preparedness.

### Results

The histopathology-based case series comprised 86 tumor submissions from 81 animals accrued between March 2022 and March 2025. Mammary tumors were the largest category (43/86; 50.0%), followed by cutaneous/subcutaneous tumors (20/86; 23.3%); 80 tumors (93.0%) were classified as malignant.

Among 162 questionnaire responses collected between October 2024 and May 2025, 111 respondents selected “dogs and cats” as their main animal group. Mammary tumors were reported by 109 respondents (98.2%), cutaneous/subcutaneous tumors by 79 (71.2%), and canine transmissible venereal tumor (CTVT) by 54 (48.6%); multiple categories could be reported. The most frequent self-reported preparedness rating was “Moderately prepared” (52/111; 46.8%), while 99 of 110 respondents with valid data (90.0%) rated diagnostic resources as either “Insufficient” or “Not at all satisfactory.”

Mammary and cutaneous/subcutaneous tumors ranked first and second in both sources, whereas the rankings of the remaining categories differed. Because the sources represented different populations, analytical units, denominators, and diagnostic pathways, the comparison was restricted to an exploratory descriptive assessment and was not interpreted as evidence of differences in population-level tumor occurrence.

### Conclusions

This study provides an initial structured account of companion-animal tumor documentation in Algeria. The partial agreement between the two sources, together with unfavorable diagnostic-availability ratings, suggests potential gaps between clinical recognition, histopathological confirmation, and systematic recording. Standardized submission and coding procedures, improved specimen-transport and formal pathology-referral pathways, broader geographic participation, and progressive development of companion-animal cancer registration are needed to strengthen the national evidence base.

## Methods

### Overall study design

This dual-source descriptive study comprised two independently analyzed components: a histopathology-based case series of diagnostic tumor submissions from dogs and cats received between March 2022 and March 2025; and a cross-sectional questionnaire survey of veterinarians practicing in Algeria, conducted between October 2024 and May 2025.

The histopathology component characterized tumors reaching histopathological confirmation through a diagnostic-submission pathway, whereas the questionnaire component characterized practitioner-reported tumor patterns, perceived availability of diagnostic resources, and self-reported preparedness. The two components were analyzed separately because they differed in their populations, units of analysis, sampling pathways, geographic coverage, and potential sources of bias.

The datasets were not linked at the animal, veterinarian, or practice level. Some veterinarians who submitted specimens may also have participated in the questionnaire; however, because the survey was anonymous and the datasets were unlinked, any overlap could not be identified or quantified. Cross-source comparison was therefore restricted to an exploratory descriptive assessment of broad tumor-category rankings after terminology harmonization. No direct statistical comparison between the sources was performed.

### Histopathology-based case series

From March 2022 to March 2025, diagnostic tumor submissions from dogs and cats were received. The histopathological processing and evaluation were performed at the Anatomic Pathology Laboratory, Institut des Sciences Vétérinaires El-Khroub, Université Constantine 1 Frères Mentouri. The laboratory provided study-associated diagnostic histopathology and was not part of a routine national veterinary pathology submission network. Eligible submissions originated from Constantine, Algiers, Setif, Annaba, Tebessa, and Boumerdes.

Biopsies and surgical excisions were performed by the submitting veterinarians for clinical purposes before submission. The study did not determine or modify biopsy, surgical, treatment, or other clinical-management decisions, and no additional tissue was collected for research purposes. However, no publicly available national sampling frame identified veterinarians who were actively practicing during the survey period or specifically treating companion animals. Because recruitment occurred through open professional networks, paper distribution, and peer forwarding, the number of unique eligible veterinarians reached could not be determined; consequently, a conventional response rate could not be calculated. No a priori sample-size calculation was performed because the survey was exploratory and descriptive, with no prespecified primary hypothesis, effect size, or precision target. Recruitment therefore sought the maximum feasible participation during the predefined survey period, and the resulting convenience sample was not considered nationally representative.

【turn1508news11】 [wordlim: 100] Published: 8 months ago; The University of Queensland’s Gatton campus is trialling Enzistat, an experimental cancer drug developed by US pharmaceutical company Avammune, for dogs with terminal or inoperable tumours. Professor Rachel Allavena said early company data suggests the drug may extend survival and reduce cancer-related side effects in dogs, with possible future applications for human cancer treatment. Researchers are seeking 30 dogs with inoperable tumours and 30 receiving palliative care. The trial aims to determine whether Enzistat can shrink tumours enough for surgery or improve comfort and prolong life for dogs without other curative options. Dogs must have a confirmed cancer diagnosis and veterinary referral. Participating owners will administer one tablet twice daily for six weeks and bring their dogs to UQ Gatton for three visits. The study covers the medication and specified tests, including blood work, biopsies and examinations, while owners remain responsible for other veterinary expenses. Interested owners can contact uqvets.sa@uq.edu.au.
